title: Chapter Four — the great frost, and Paradise
collection: The Life of St Andrew the Fool

sections.heading: Chapter Four — the great frost, and Paradise

pairs.en: *A grievous storm rages.* *He falls into a long trance, is caught up into heaven, and sees many things.*

**27.** A savage winter storm came on, and a cold so bitter that it gripped the air and left every living body stiff with frost. Every house was filled with snow, because the north wind blew so hard that it stripped the tiles even off the humblest houses, let alone the tall ones. The poor cried out and wailed and groaned, and wasted away between hunger and the violence of the cold, and were sent off to their deaths; others were buried under the snow and died the same way. Storage jars split apart. Trees were torn up by the roots. The birds of the sky died for want of food.

I grieved terribly for the servant of God, because his body was bare — he had no house and no hearth, no tunic, no sheepskin, no cloak, not even a haircloth, not so much as a hut. I was in real pain, not knowing what had become of him or what corner of the city he might be hiding in; and I was sure he must have died.

The violence of the winter held for many days. But when a fortnight had gone by and the great wind finally dropped and eased, late one evening this man of blessed memory, this servant of God, came to me.

When I saw him I was beside myself. I got up at once and threw my arms round him and greeted him with a holy kiss; and when we had stayed a long while in that embrace, he said: *Enough now.* *Let us sit down, my dear, and stop crying — I have something to tell you.*
And when he had sat down he said pleasantly: *Have a table laid, so we can be cheerful.* And hearing that, I gave the order.

**28.** While the boy was busy carrying it out, the righteous man said to me: *Truly, my lord and sweetest brother, why were you so distressed about me?* *Did you suppose I had died of the cold like all my brothers, the poor?* *Do you not know that the Lord keeps those who love him — that the Lord is near to the broken-hearted, and saves the humble in spirit?* *Do you not know that the one who said to my wretchedness, “If you love me with your whole soul, you shall know my gifts,” promised also the great comfort that comes from him?* *Never think such a thing about me again, my friend.* *Great is the joy of those who hope in God with their whole soul, both in this age and in the age to come.*

Hearing this, it came into my mind that some wonder must have been worked on him in such an extremity, and that this was why he was speaking to me so. So I began, with the gentlest words, kissing him and smoothing the way, and asked him plainly: *My lord, how did you get through those days?* *I adjure you by the God of heaven and earth — do not hide from me what God has worked in you.*
**29.** And the blessed man said: *My friend in the Lord, where should a fool who is out of his senses have spent his time, except in his folly and his mockeries, as he always does?*

*And yet, my brother, your love sets me on fire, and a great longing pulls me to confess it to you.* *But I adjure you by the God who made all things by his word, together with his only-begotten Son our Lord Jesus Christ and his holy and life-giving Spirit: as long as I am alive, tell this to nobody at all.* *And out of the burning love I have for you, I will tell you openly.*
When I had bound myself by the most solemn oath to keep his charge, then he opened his precious mouth and said:

*You know, beloved, how violent that cold and that great wind were — it did not escape you, my dearest, how hard it pressed on us.* *I could think of no plan.* *I had no clothes and no shelter, and nowhere to lay my head.* *So I went to look for safety among the poor, my own kind, and they would not have me: they drove me off with sticks like a dog, loathing me and saying “Get out of here, dog!” — and I went away.* *There was nowhere I could be safe, and every hope of living left me.* *And I said: “Blessed is the Lord God.* *It is no strange thing if I die for love of him.* *But God is not unjust; he will set a limit to this cold too, and give me the patience to bear it.”*

**30.** *So I went off to a corner of one of the porticoes, and finding a little dog there I lay down close against it, hoping to get some warmth from it.* *But when it saw me beside it, it got up and moved away.*

*Then I said to myself: “Wretch, do you see what a sinner you are?* *Even the dogs run from you and will not have you, not even as one of their own kind.* *Men turn from you as from an evil spirit, dogs find you disgusting, the poor drive you off — what is left for you to claim?* *You are dying, madman, you are dying; there is no safety for you here.”*

*And as I said this in anguish, compunction came over me; and gripped by the cold and by that violent shivering I wept, looking towards God only with the eyes of my mind.* *And when every limb had gone cold, I thought I was about to breathe my last.*

*Then all at once I became aware of a warmth.* *I opened my eyes, and I saw a young man of extraordinary beauty, his face flashing like the sun; and he held in his hand a golden branch woven with roses and lilies still wet with dew — not the kind this world has, God forbid, but of some other growing and some other flowering.*
*While I was gazing at that beautiful branch in his hand, he looked at me and said: “Andrew, where were you?”*
*I said: “In darkness, and in the shadow of death.”*
*And he said: “How so?” — and with the word he struck me across the face with that flowering branch and said: “Let your body receive life that cannot be overcome.”*
*At once the fragrance of those flowers went into my heart, and like a flash of lightning it put life into me.*
*And after that I heard a voice saying: “Take him away to a place of refreshment for two weeks, and then he shall come back; for I say he has still to contend.”*

*And with the word I was caught up into a deep and most sweet sleep, and I did not know what became of me.* *Just as a man sleeps sweetly through a whole night, so it was with me through those two weeks, in whatever place the will of God appointed.*

**31.** *But finding myself in a Paradise, delightful and past all wonder, I was beside myself.* *And I reasoned with myself what this could be — I knew my home was in Constantinople, but what I was doing here I could not understand.*

*Marvelling greatly at the thing, and how it had come about, I said in my perplexity: “See how truly I am out of my senses!* *A good thing has come to me from God, and I ought to be glorifying him and giving thanks — and here I sit, prying into this astonishing wonder.”*
*And I seemed to myself to have no flesh at all;* *I did not think I was wearing a body.*

*I was wearing a tunic that flashed with light, white as snow and set with gems, and I took great delight in the beauty of it.* *And I noticed what was on my head, and there was a crown on me woven out of every kind of flower; and there were sandals on my feet —*
**32.** *— and I was belted with a belt of a colour dyed to strike awe into you, a deep hue, something like purple.*

*The air of that indescribable Paradise was rich with all kinds of flowers whose colours never faded; and a fragrance of many kinds, always changing, met my senses in a way strange and delightful.* *Believe me, my mind shudders as I tell you this.* *I was like a king who has everything he could want, moving about that garden, taking great delight in myself, my mind feeding on the sight of things that had grown there by a power beyond anything human.*

*For the place put out in abundance what God had made spring up there — nothing this world enjoys, far from it, but of an altogether different nature: always green, fragrant, thick with leaves, dripping with honey, high-crowned, their branches bending over and waving against one another, a sight beyond pleasure and beyond sense itself.* *Blessed are those whose souls are filled with the sight of such gladness.*

*And this was strange: on some there were flowers only; on others the beauty went further; and to others it was given to bear leaves and fruit of many kinds at once, without ever stopping.* *On some there was blossom, and leaves, and something wonderful to see, and precious fruit, admired from every side.*

*And there was a very great wonder in them, for there were sparrows on them too, and other beautiful birds, each after its own name — some golden-winged, others of many colours, sitting one on every leaf.* *And they were singing and warbling, so that I think their beautiful voices could be heard rising to the topmost heaven.* *And I took those sparrows for angels of heaven, and the astonishing sight of all their variety carried my mind away.*

*They were not roses, nor lilies, nor could I say what else they were, but flowers of every colour.* *Such were those birds — so strange and rare to look at, and their fruit precious, admired from every side.*

**33.** *Turning back to the beauty of the first little bird, I marvelled at it, gathering my whole mind onto that one alone; and then I fixed my thought on another, which had a great richness of some different glory and shape.* *And again I saw another, more remarkable still, which was a great delight to me.* *And their song went on without stopping, and was sweeter than anything.* *Who could describe the strange and awe-inspiring beauty of what is there?*
*Those beautiful plants stood each in its proper order, like one battle line facing another.* *How blessed the hand that planted them!*

*And going on further into the inner parts of Paradise — for I thought I was no longer in the darkness of this world; set beside what is there, the things here seemed to me darkness — as I came out into an open space, I looked, and behold, a great river ran through the middle of Paradise, and quietly watered all those plants, lapping at their roots; and those beautiful birds would come down to it, singing without stopping.*

*And a vine was spread out around the river, its leaves gleaming like gold and its shoots lovely; and I likened it to a lamp, because of the one who said “I am the true vine,” and who is the chief cornerstone, the stone hewn from the rock.* *It was spread through the whole of Paradise and laden with the largest and most beautiful clusters, so that the plants there were crowned all about by the winding of its branches.*
**34.** *Seeing all this, my heart was delighted, and my soul was carried out of awe into wonder, and out of wonder into ecstasy.*

*And when I had stood a long while without a word, I heard the sound of a wind blowing from the east and falling on the trees, making them ripple and sending out a breath of fragrance beyond describing; and delighting in it, and astonished, I took that fragrance to be the incense of God, of the kind the angels burn before his face.*

*When that wind had dropped, I heard from the west the sound of another breath, working in me a sweetness there is no tracing, whose breathing rose like vapour and had the look of snow.* *And the beauty of the trees there was filled with a fragrance more wonderful than all the spices on earth, sending out its scent from far off — a thing awesome and dear to the heart at once — so that I forgot those precious wonders I had already enjoyed on my way through, that seemed to flow with honey.*
*And as for those little birds, singing and warbling and chirping their songs of gladness, my mind went out of me.* *Whether they were birds or angels, the Lord knows.*

*Then from the north there rose another wind, most extraordinary, fiery to look at, like the rays of the sun setting in a rainbow; and as it blew with a boundless calm, those most radiant plants swayed gently, and it stirred up the sweet scent that is in the roses — so that for a long while I was carried out of my mind and went on delighting in that dearest sweetness and longing; and being almost out of my senses, after being wonderfully delighted for a long time by its pleasantness, I was seized with a violent joy at the loveliness of the fragrance that came from that wind.*
